cards.front: State the rule that sets how much fluid flows through a vessel, in words and as an equation.
cards.back: Fluid flows down a pressure difference; flow equals that difference divided by the resistance in the way: Q = (P_in − P_out) / R.
cards.quote: Fluid flows down a pressure difference, and how much flows is that difference divided by the resistance in the way

cards.front: In mammals, why is the pulmonary artery called an artery even though it carries oxygen-poor blood?
cards.back: Vessel names describe direction, not oxygen: arteries carry blood away from the heart, veins toward it.
cards.quote: The names describe direction, not oxygen: in mammals the pulmonary artery carries oxygen-poor blood away from the heart

cards.front: Why does arterial pressure never fall to zero between heartbeats?
cards.back: Artery walls contain elastic fibres; their elastic recoil between beats keeps pushing blood forward.
cards.quote: Their elastic recoil between beats keeps pushing blood forward, so arterial pressure never falls to zero.

cards.front: When arteriole smooth muscle contracts the arteriole narrows, called {{c1::vasoconstriction}}.
cards.back: When it relaxes the arteriole widens: vasodilation.
cards.quote: When it contracts (vasoconstriction) the arteriole narrows; when it relaxes (vasodilation) it widens.

cards.front: The arterioles of one organ relax (vasodilation) while the pressure difference across the organ stays the same. What happens to the organ's blood flow, and why?
cards.back: Flow rises. Wider arterioles have a much lower resistance (about 1/r^4), and at a fixed pressure difference Q = ΔP / R.
cards.why: Arterioles hold most of the circulation's resistance, so their radius is the main lever on organ flow.
cards.quote: Arterioles have walls dominated by smooth muscle.

cards.front: Why does exchange between blood and tissue fluid happen at the capillaries?
cards.back: The capillary wall is a single layer of endothelial cells on a thin basement membrane; little else separates blood from tissue fluid.
cards.quote: Capillaries have a wall of a single layer of endothelial cells, the flat cells that line every vessel, on a thin basement membrane.

cards.front: Compliance is the {{c1::change in volume per change in pressure}}.
cards.back: Veins are more compliant than arteries, so in adult humans at rest most of the blood is in the veins.
cards.quote: compliance is the change in volume per change in pressure, so they hold much more blood for a small rise in pressure

cards.front: What is the muscle pump, and how does it move venous blood?
cards.back: Contracting muscles squeeze limb veins; one-way valves in the veins make the squeezed blood move toward the heart.
cards.quote: Many limb veins have one-way valves; contracting muscles squeeze them and push blood toward the heart: the muscle pump.

cards.front: Poiseuille's law for steady flow through a rigid tube: R = 8 × viscosity × length / (π × {{c1::radius^4}})
cards.back: An idealization: blood is not a simple fluid and vessels are not rigid.
cards.quote: R = 8 × viscosity × length / (π × radius^4)

cards.front: In an adult human at rest (illustrative numbers), mean arterial pressure is 93 mmHg, right atrial pressure 3 mmHg and cardiac output 5.0 L per min. Calculate total peripheral resistance.
cards.why: Rearranges Q = ΔP / R, treating the whole body as one resistance.
cards.quote: Total peripheral resistance = (93 − 3) / 5.0 = 90 / 5.0 = 18 mmHg min per L.

cards.front: One arteriole's radius halves; its length, blood viscosity and the pressure difference across it are unchanged. By Poiseuille's idealization, what fraction of the original flow remains?
cards.back: Resistance rises 2^4 = 16 times, so flow falls to 1/16, or 6.25 percent.
cards.why: Answering one half means treating resistance as proportional to 1/r instead of 1/r^4.
cards.quote: Its resistance rises 2^4 = 16 times, so its flow falls to 1/16, or 6.25 percent.

cards.front: Every arteriole in one organ halves its radius. The arterioles held half the organ's resistance, and the pressure across the organ is fixed. Does the organ's flow fall to 1/16?
cards.back: No. Series resistances add: 0.5 × 16 + 0.5 = 8.5 times the old resistance, so organ flow falls to 1/8.5, about 12 percent.
cards.why: One sixteenth describes the narrowed vessels, not the whole organ.
cards.quote: the organ's resistance becomes 8.5 times the old and its flow falls to 1/8.5, about 12 percent

cards.front: In an organ, the arterioles hold 75 percent of the resistance and the rest of the vessels 25 percent, in series. Every arteriole halves its radius; the pressure across the organ is fixed. What fraction of the original organ flow remains?
cards.back: New resistance = 0.75 × 16 + 0.25 = 12.25 times the old, so flow falls to 1/12.25, about 8 percent.
cards.why: Rests on Poiseuille's 1/r^4 and on series resistances adding; the larger the arterioles' share, the closer the organ comes to 1/16.
cards.quote: Resistances in a chain (in series) add.

cards.front: Why does narrowing a single arteriole, among many arranged side by side in an organ, change the organ's total flow very little?
cards.back: The paths are in parallel: flow divides among them, and the many unchanged arterioles still carry blood, so the organ's total resistance barely changes.
cards.quote: Narrowing a single arteriole among many side by side would change the organ's flow very little.

cards.front: For paths side by side (in parallel), n equal paths resist {{c1::1/n}} as much as one.
cards.back: The flow divides among them.
cards.quote: the flow divides, so n equal paths resist 1/n as much as one
cards.section: Narrowest, but not the main resistance

cards.front: With a made-up figure, one capillary resists 50 times as much as one arteriole. What is the resistance of 100 such capillaries side by side, relative to one arteriole, and what does this show?
cards.back: 50 / 100 = 0.5, half as much as one arteriole. The narrowest vessels are not the main resistance, because so many lie in parallel.
cards.why: A sketch of the logic only: real beds also branch and rejoin.
cards.quote: if one capillary resisted 50 times as much as one arteriole, 100 side by side would resist half as much
cards.section: Narrowest, but not the main resistance

cards.front: Using made-up round numbers, a volume flow of about 83 cm^3 per s passes through an aorta of 4 cm^2 and through capillaries totalling 3,000 cm^2. Calculate the mean velocity in each and explain the difference.
cards.back: Aorta: 83 / 4 ≈ 21 cm per s. Capillaries: 83 / 3,000 ≈ 0.03 cm per s. The same flow spreads over the largest total cross-section, so blood is slowest in capillaries.
cards.quote: 83 / 4 cm^2 of aorta is about 21 cm per s, and 83 / 3,000 cm^2 of capillaries is about 0.03 cm per s
cards.section: Narrowest, but not the main resistance

cards.front: Oncotic pressure is the osmotic pull of proteins that cross the capillary wall poorly; in mammals it comes mostly from {{c1::albumin}}.
cards.quote: π for oncotic pressure (the osmotic pull of proteins that cross the wall poorly, in mammals mostly albumin)

cards.front: Write the net Starling pressure across a capillary wall (outward positive), assuming protein cannot cross the wall.
cards.back: net pressure = (P_c − P_i) − (π_c − π_i): hydrostatic push out minus oncotic pull in, each capillary minus interstitial.
cards.quote: net pressure = (P_c − P_i) − (π_c − π_i)

cards.front: A single perfused microvessel has protein inside, very little outside, and outside pressure near zero. Fluid flux across the wall (outward positive) is −1, 0 and +1 (arbitrary units) at capillary pressures of 15, 25 and 35 mmHg. Estimate the effective oncotic pressure and the wall's hydraulic conductance.
cards.back: Flux is zero at 25 mmHg, so the effective oncotic pressure is about 25 mmHg. Slope = 2 / 20 = 0.1 units per mmHg, the conductance K.
cards.why: Flux = net pressure / wall resistance; with outside terms near zero, net pressure = P_c − effective oncotic pressure.
cards.quote: Flow across the wall is this net pressure divided by the wall's resistance to water: the one idea again.

cards.front: Classic model, illustrative adult human numbers: capillary pressure 35 mmHg at the arterial end and 15 mmHg at the venous end, interstitial pressure 0, plasma oncotic 25 mmHg, interstitial oncotic 3 mmHg. Find the net pressure at each end (outward positive).
cards.back: Oncotic difference = 25 − 3 = 22 mmHg. Arterial end: 35 − 22 = +13 mmHg, outward. Venous end: 15 − 22 = −7 mmHg, inward.
cards.quote: Arterial end: 35 − 22 = +13 mmHg, outward. Venous end: 15 − 22 = −7 mmHg, inward.

cards.front: Why is capillary blood pressure lower at the venous end than at the arterial end?
cards.back: Pressure drops along the capillary's own resistance as blood flows through it (Q = ΔP / R applied along the vessel).
cards.quote: falling to 15 mmHg at the venous end as pressure drops along the capillary's own resistance

cards.front: Classic model numbers (capillary pressure 35 mmHg arterial end, 15 mmHg venous end, interstitial pressure 0, interstitial oncotic 3 mmHg), but plasma oncotic pressure falls from 25 to 12.5 mmHg. Find the net pressure at each end and predict the tissue outcome.
cards.back: Oncotic difference = 12.5 − 3 = 9.5 mmHg. Arterial end: 35 − 9.5 = +25.5; venous end: 15 − 9.5 = +5.5 mmHg, both outward. Filtration rises along the whole capillary; tissue fluid accumulates if lymph cannot keep up.
cards.why: Rests on net pressure = (P_c − P_i) − (π_c − π_i) and on lymph as the return route.
cards.quote: plasma oncotic pressure 25 mmHg; interstitial oncotic pressure 3 mmHg

cards.front: What is the glycocalyx of a capillary?
cards.back: A sugar-rich coat on the inner surface of the endothelium that holds back protein.
cards.quote: the glycocalyx, a sugar-rich coat on the inner surface of the endothelium that holds back protein
cards.section: What survives, and what does not

cards.front: In the revised Starling view, why does protein in average tissue fluid not cancel the plasma's oncotic pull?
cards.back: The difference that matters lies across the glycocalyx, between plasma and the fluid just beneath the coat (π_sub), which has less protein than average tissue fluid.
cards.quote: That fluid has less protein than average tissue fluid, so tissue protein does not cancel the pull.
cards.section: What survives, and what does not

cards.front: In perfused rat mesenteric microvessels, albumin was made equal in plasma and tissue. What happened to the effective oncotic opposition to filtration, and what does it show?
cards.back: It stayed near 70 percent of the plasma oncotic pressure inside the vessel. Bulk tissue protein does not set the opposing pull; the fluid beneath the glycocalyx does.
cards.quote: the effective oncotic opposition stayed near 70 percent of the plasma oncotic pressure inside the vessel, even with equal albumin in plasma and tissue
cards.section: What survives, and what does not

cards.front: Revised model, illustrative: effective oncotic pull 17.5 mmHg, interstitial pressure 0. Which way does fluid move at a capillary pressure of 35 mmHg, and at 15 mmHg, and does the second last?
cards.back: At 35 mmHg: 35 − 17.5 = +17.5 mmHg, outward. At 15 mmHg: 15 − 17.5 = −2.5 mmHg, inward, but only for a while.
cards.why: Water drawn in concentrates the protein beneath the coat, the pull shrinks, and absorption fades.
cards.quote: At 15 mmHg it is 15 − 17.5 = −2.5 mmHg, inward, but only for a while.
cards.section: What survives, and what does not

cards.front: The giraffe's feet lie far below its heart. Using the Starling balance, explain how two of its reported leg defences, narrowing of the small vessels that feed the capillaries and capillary walls that let little plasma protein through, limit fluid build-up.
cards.back: By the Starling balance, narrowing the feeding vessels would be expected to add resistance upstream, so more pressure is dropped before the capillaries and P_c is lower. Little protein leaking out would be expected to keep the oncotic pull opposing filtration high.
cards.why: Rests on Q = ΔP / R along vessels in series and on net pressure = (P_c − P_i) − (π_c − π_i).
cards.quote: narrowing of the small vessels that feed the capillaries; and capillary walls that let little plasma protein through
cards.section: What survives, and what does not

cards.front: Filtered fluid enters blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and is then called {{c1::lymph}}.
cards.quote: Filtered fluid enters blind-ended lymphatic capillaries and is then called lymph.

cards.front: In mouse trachea, how do the junctions of lymphatic capillaries differ from those of larger collecting lymphatics, and what is the proposed role of the first?
cards.back: Lymphatic capillaries have short "buttons" with loose, overlapping flaps, thought (from structure alone) to let fluid in but not out; collecting vessels have continuous "zipper" junctions and valves.
cards.quote: In mouse trachea their cells are joined by short "buttons" with loose, overlapping flaps between them

cards.front: Frogs pump lymph into veins with lymph hearts; mammals have none. What moves lymph in mammals?
cards.back: Collecting lymphatic walls contract, body movements squeeze them, and valves keep lymph moving one way, much as the muscle pump moves venous blood.
cards.quote: The walls of mammalian collecting lymphatics contract, body movements squeeze them, and their valves keep lymph moving one way

cards.front: In humans, where does lymph re-enter the blood?
cards.back: Where the jugular and subclavian veins join in the neck, after passing through lymph nodes.
cards.quote: in humans it re-enters the blood where the jugular and subclavian veins join in the neck

cards.front: The lymphatics draining a mammalian tissue are blocked while its capillary blood pressure stays the same. Predict what happens to tissue fluid and to leaked plasma protein.
cards.back: Tissue fluid accumulates, and leaked protein builds up, because capillaries filter fluid and lymph is the main route returning filtrate and protein to the blood.
cards.quote: Leaked protein comes back mainly this way.

cards.front: In the small intestine, lymphatics called {{c1::lacteals}} carry absorbed fat.
cards.quote: In the small intestine, lymphatics called lacteals carry absorbed fat

cards.front: Platelets are cell fragments shed by large cells called {{c1::megakaryocytes}}.
cards.quote: Platelets are cell fragments shed by large cells called megakaryocytes.
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells is the {{c1::hematocrit}}.
cards.back: In adult humans roughly 36 to 54 percent, lower in women than in men.
cards.quote: The fraction of blood volume made up of red cells is the hematocrit
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: How do mammalian red cells differ from those of birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish, and what replaces platelets in those other vertebrates?
cards.back: Mammalian red cells lose their nucleus as they mature; the others keep it (rare exceptions, such as a few salamanders). Other vertebrates have nucleated thrombocytes instead of platelets.
cards.quote: Mammalian red cells lose their nucleus as they mature; those of birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish keep it
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: List the overlapping steps of hemostasis in mammals, in order.
cards.back: Vascular spasm, platelet plug, coagulation, clot contraction, fibrinolysis (plasmin breaks the fibrin down).
cards.quote: Hemostasis, stopping blood loss, runs in overlapping steps in mammals
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: How does vascular spasm help stop blood loss from a cut vessel?
cards.back: The vessel's smooth muscle contracts; narrowing steeply raises the resistance of the path out (roughly the 1/r^4 lever), so less blood escapes.
cards.quote: Narrowing steeply raises the resistance of the path out (the 1/r^4 lever, roughly: a wound is no ideal tube).
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: Coagulation ends with the enzyme {{c1::thrombin}} converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands.
cards.back: It starts when tissue factor, exposed at the injury, triggers a chain of enzymes.
cards.quote: It ends with the enzyme thrombin converting soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin strands.
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: Why is coagulation built as a cascade, a chain of enzymes, rather than a single step?
cards.back: A cascade amplifies a small start (tissue factor at the injury) into a large output (much fibrin).
cards.quote: A cascade amplifies a small start into a large output, the logic of signaling circuits.
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: In human plasma clots in vitro, platelets are prevented from attaching to fibrin. Predict the effect on clot compaction, and why.
cards.back: Compaction falls. Clot contraction depends on platelet extensions pulling on fibrin fibres; without attachment they cannot pull.
cards.quote: platelet extensions pull on fibrin fibres and compact the clot
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: What did Levin and Bang find about horseshoe crab (Limulus) blood, and how does its clot differ from a mammal's?
cards.back: Bacterial endotoxin makes amebocyte material clot. Amebocytes store clotting factors in granules, and the cascade ends in the gel protein coagulin, not fibrin.
cards.quote: Levin and Bang (1964) reported that bacterial endotoxin makes amebocyte material clot
cards.section: Blood and stopping a leak, compared across animals

cards.front: Design a measurement in single microvessels that distinguishes steady venous-end reabsorption (classic model) from transient absorption (revised model).
cards.back: Measure filtration in the first seconds after a pressure drop and again after many minutes. The revised model predicts absorption fades as protein beneath the glycocalyx evens out; the classic model predicts it lasts.
cards.why: Also measure oncotic pressure as close to the outside of the endothelium as possible, and repeat in another tissue.
cards.quote: measure filtration in the first seconds after a pressure step and again after many minutes

cards.front: Blocking a tissue's lymphatics makes it swell. Why can this result not decide between the classic and revised models of capillary exchange?
cards.back: Swelling shows net filtration, but the classic model also leaves a small filtrate for lymph, so both models predict swelling.
cards.quote: swelling shows net filtration, but the classic model also leaves a small filtrate for lymph, so swelling cannot tell the models apart

cards.front: In the full Starling relation, what is the reflection coefficient σ, and what are its limiting values?
cards.back: The reflection coefficient for protein: 1 if protein cannot cross the wall at all, 0 if it crosses freely. It scales the oncotic term.
cards.quote: σ is the reflection coefficient for protein: 1 if protein cannot cross at all, 0 if it crosses freely

cards.front: Damage makes a capillary wall let protein through more freely (σ falls toward 0), with capillary and interstitial pressures unchanged. Predict the change in fluid flux and explain.
cards.back: Outward fluid flux rises. In J_v = K × [(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π_sub)], a smaller σ shrinks the oncotic term opposing filtration.
cards.why: Rests on the full Starling relation; adds no new facts.
cards.quote: In full, J_v = K × [(P_c − P_i) − σ(π_c − π_sub)]
